title: Drawing lines, circles and filling regions
kicker: ENCT 201 · Computer Graphics and Visualization · Chapter 2 (output primitives)
subtitle: A screen has only whole pixels. These are the classic ways to choose which ones to light.

sections.title: The DDA line algorithm
sections.body:
Draw a straight line from one point to another on graph paper, using only whole squares. Which squares do you colour? You walk along the line and, at each step, pick the nearest square. The DDA (digital differential analyser) does precisely this.

It steps along the longer axis one pixel at a time and adds the slope to the other coordinate, rounding each point: steps = max(|Δx|, |Δy|), x increment = Δx/steps, y increment = Δy/steps. Why the longer axis? So that no gaps are left in the line. Run it from (0,0) to (4,2): Δx = 4 and Δy = 2, so steps = 4, with x += 1 and y += 0.5. The points are (0,0), (1,0.5→1), (2,1), (3,1.5→2), (4,2), and it lights 0,0 1,1 2,1 3,2 4,2. The catch is that it uses floating point and rounding inside the loop, which is slow.

worked.why: Line from (0,0) to (4,2): Δx = 4, Δy = 2, so steps = 4.

questions.prompt: Why does DDA step along the longer axis?

choices.text: So the other coordinate changes by at most 1 per step and no gaps appear.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Each step moves one pixel in the major direction.

figures.caption: Figure 2.1.1 — DDA from (2,2) to (13,8)
figures.note: Each frame rounds one point to a pixel.

keynotes: DDA steps along the longer axis one pixel at a time and adds the slope to the other coordinate, rounding each point.
steps = max(|Δx|, |Δy|), with x increment Δx/steps and y increment Δy/steps.
From (0,0) to (4,2) it lights 0,0 1,1 2,1 3,2 4,2; it uses floating point and rounding in the loop.

sections.title: Bresenham’s line algorithm
sections.body:
Can we draw the same line without any fractions at all? Yes, and that was Bresenham’s clever insight. Bresenham keeps an integer decision (error) term that says whether the ideal line is closer to the pixel straight ahead or the one diagonally above. Each step, you look at the sign of the term and move accordingly.

No multiplication, no rounding: only additions and sign tests, which is why it lives inside hardware. From (0,0) to (5,2) it lights 0,0 1,0 2,1 3,1 4,2 5,2. The main advantage over DDA? Integer arithmetic only. The error term decides each step, as the figure shows.

questions.prompt: The main advantage of Bresenham over DDA is…

responses.title: Close, but not it.
responses.body: It is exact in choosing pixels.

figures.caption: Figure 2.2.1 — Bresenham from (2,2) to (13,8)
figures.note: The error term decides each step.

keynotes: Bresenham keeps an integer decision (error) term saying whether the ideal line is closer to the pixel straight ahead or the one diagonally above.
It uses only additions and sign tests, no multiplication or rounding, hence its use in hardware.

sections.title: The mid-point circle algorithm
sections.body:
A circle is the most symmetrical shape there is, so why compute all of it? Because it is symmetric about both axes and the diagonals, you only need one octant (x from 0 to y), then reflect each point 8 ways. That is an eight-fold saving for free.

The mid-point method decides each step by testing whether the midpoint between the two candidate pixels is inside the circle, using a decision parameter p. Start p₀ = 1 − r; if p < 0 keep y and p += 2x + 1, else y−− and p += 2(x − y) + 1. Try radius 5: p₀ = 1 − 5 = −4. Start (0,5). p < 0, so x = 1, y = 5, p = −4 + 2(1) + 1 = −1. Again p < 0, so x = 2, p = −1 + 5 = 4. Now p ≥ 0, so y = 4 at x = 3. The first octant is 0,5 1,5 2,5 3,4. Each frame of the figure plots eight points at once.

questions.prompt: Why compute only one octant of a circle?

choices.text: Symmetry gives the other seven octants by reflecting coordinates.

keynotes: A circle is symmetric, so compute one octant (x from 0 to y) and reflect each point 8 ways.
The mid-point method uses a decision parameter: p₀ = 1 − r; if p < 0 keep y and p += 2x + 1, else y−− and p += 2(x − y) + 1.
For r = 5 the first octant is 0,5 1,5 2,5 3,4.

sections.title: Filling: scan-line, boundary and flood fill
sections.body:
Outlines are only half the job; you also want to colour the inside. There are two families of approach. Scan-line fill walks down the picture row by row, intersects each row with the polygon edges, and fills between pairs of crossings (the odd–even rule). Boundary fill starts inside and spreads like spilled paint until it meets a boundary colour; flood fill spreads through all pixels of the old colour.

Spreading needs a notion of neighbour. You can use 4-connected neighbours (up, down, left, right) or 8-connected (plus diagonals). Beware: 8-connected fill can leak through a diagonal gap in a boundary drawn with 4-connected lines, like water finding a crack. The default pentagon fills 61 pixels. Watch the fill spread from the seed to the boundary in the figure.

questions.prompt: Which fill can leak through a diagonal gap in the boundary?

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: It also moves diagonally, through the gap.

figures.caption: Figure 2.4.1 — 4-connected flood fill
figures.note: The fill spreads from the seed to the boundary.

keynotes: Scan-line fill intersects each row with the polygon edges and fills between pairs of crossings (odd–even rule).
Boundary fill spreads until it meets a boundary colour; flood fill spreads through all pixels of the old colour.
4-connected uses up, down, left and right; 8-connected adds diagonals and can leak through a diagonal gap.

sections.title: Aliasing and antialiasing
sections.body:
Draw a gently slanted line and, when you zoom in, you will see it looks like a staircase. Those jagged steps (“jaggies”) are aliasing, the price of using discrete pixels for a continuous world.

Antialiasing softens them. One way is to supersample: compute at a higher resolution and average. Another is to shade edge pixels in proportion to how much of the pixel the line covers. The cost, as ever, is more computation. Supersampling works by averaging several samples per pixel.

choices.text: Renders at a higher resolution and averages down.

problems.prompt: A line has slope 0.3. Does Bresenham step mostly in x or in y?
problems.answer: |slope| < 1, so x is the major axis: x advances every step and y increases by 1 about 3 times in 10 steps.

keynotes: Aliasing is the stepped look of slanted lines caused by discrete pixels.
Antialiasing supersamples (compute at higher resolution and average) or shades edge pixels in proportion to the coverage.

sections.title: Summary
sections.body:
A quick recap before you move on.

  • DDA: float increments; Bresenham: integers; circle: one octant + symmetry.
  • Fill by scan line, boundary or flood (4 vs 8 connectivity).

Notice the theme: each algorithm is a way of getting the same picture with less work. That is graphics in a sentence.
keynotes: DDA uses float increments, Bresenham uses integers, and a circle needs only one octant plus symmetry.
Fill by scan line, boundary or flood, with 4- or 8-connectivity.
